title: Watch: Australian Dolphin Filmed Catching Fish with Shells
gist: A new Marine Mammal Science study documents 'shelling' — dolphins lifting large conch shells to drain water and eat trapped fish — for the first time in an Eastern Australian dolphin population, previously known only from Western Australia.

insights.claim: Fifteen years ago, a note in the journal Marine Mammal Science first documented Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops sp.) in Western Australia lifting large conch shells from the water by sticking their noses into the openings.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Establishes the prior baseline discovery (Western Australia, 15 years ago) against which this new Eastern Australia observation is a geographic extension.
insights.quote: Fifteen years ago, a note in the journal Marine Mammal Science commented on an odd behavior of dolphins in Western Australia.

insights.claim: The purpose of 'shelling' behavior was revealed to be dolphins shaking a lifted conch shell to drain the water out and eat a fish trapped inside, and multiple instances of this behavior have since been observed in Western Australian dolphins.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Confirms 'shelling' as a genuine foraging tool-use technique rather than incidental behavior, adding to the evidence base for dolphin cognitive sophistication.
insights.quote: The purpose of this “shelling” was revealed when dolphins shook the shell to drain water out of it and eat a fish that had been trapped inside.

insights.claim: A new study in Marine Mammal Science reports the first documentation of shelling behavior in an Eastern Australian dolphin population, based on footage of two instances captured by researchers plus reports from a dolphin tour company.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Extends the known geographic range of this dolphin tool-use behavior to a new, previously undocumented population in Eastern Australia.
insights.quote: Now, a new study in Marine Mammal Science reports shelling in another dolphin population, this time in Eastern Australia.

insights.claim: Lead study author Alexis Levengood, a marine mammal biologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast, described spotting a dolphin raising something large out of the water during a research boat trip and immediately recognizing it as shelling behavior.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Provides a firsthand researcher account establishing how the Eastern Australian shelling observation was made and identified in the field.
insights.quote: “We were on a research boat … when we spotted a dolphin raising something large out of the water,” said lead study author Alexis Levengood, a marine mammal biologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast, in a press release. “I started screaming because I know what shelling looks like.”
insights.locator: We were on a research boat
